flashcards.q: In a worked 2-second RAG budget, roughly how is time allocated across stages?
flashcards.a: ~75ms embedding, ~100ms ANN retrieval, ~250ms rerank (top~100), ~75ms buffer, leaving ~1500ms (~75% of total) for generation, which dominates because it's the least compressible stage.

flashcards.q: What is the cascade retrieval pattern and why is it structured that way?
flashcards.a: Stage 1: cheap, wide hybrid ANN retrieval (top 50-150) optimized for recall. Stage 2: expensive, narrow cross-encoder rerank (top 3-20) optimized for precision. Works because stage-1 cost is roughly independent of top-k, while stage-2 cost scales linearly with candidate count and can't run over the whole corpus at interactive latency.

flashcards.q: What are typical latencies for query embedding and cross-encoder reranking?
flashcards.a: Query embedding: 50-100ms (e.g. Voyage lite ~52ms/query). Cross-encoder rerank: 100-300ms via Cohere's hosted API, or ~50ms/pair for self-hosted BGE-reranker-v2-m3 on an L40S GPU.

flashcards.q: What three costs does retrieving more candidates (higher top-k) incur?
flashcards.a: 1) Reranker latency/cost scales linearly with candidate count. 2) Generation context-token cost scales linearly with candidates passed to the LLM. 3) Quality can drop past a threshold via the "lost in the middle" effect -- more context doesn't guarantee better attention to the right part of it.

flashcards.q: Do retrieval-quality techniques (hybrid, contextual retrieval, reranking, reformulation) stack additively in accuracy?
flashcards.a: No. Evidence shows rerank-over-hybrid often matches rerank-over-dense-only, meaning the reranker's gain subsumes much of the hybrid leg's contribution. Precision returns flatten while latency costs of each added stage stay additive.

flashcards.q: When should you cut the reranking stage?
flashcards.a: When stage-1 recall is already sufficient (eval-verified), when the latency budget can't afford 100-300ms (sub-500ms targets), when the corpus is small/low-noise, or when reranking cost at your actual QPS doesn't pencil out economically.

flashcards.q: What is Cohere Rerank's approximate pricing and latency?
flashcards.a: Roughly $0.001-$0.0025 per search of up to 100 documents (documents over 500 tokens split into additional billed sub-chunks); typical latency 100-300ms.

flashcards.q: What's the discipline for deciding a retrieval-pipeline change is actually an improvement?
flashcards.a: 1) Offline eval (recall@k/nDCG) to gate cheaply. 2) Shadow/canary deployment to measure real p50/p99 latency under load. 3) Online A/B test on a user-facing metric (task success, feedback, follow-up-query rate) since offline recall improving doesn't guarantee the online metric moves.

flashcards.q: Why does generation typically dominate the RAG latency budget?
flashcards.a: Generation latency is driven by output token count and model size/architecture, mostly outside retrieval's control -- often 60-75% of total budget vs the much smaller slices spent on embedding, ANN search, and reranking.

flashcards.q: What is the "lost in the middle" effect and why does it matter for retrieval budget decisions?
flashcards.a: Models exhibit degraded attention to information buried in the middle of a long context. It means blindly adding more retrieved chunks "to be safe" can measurably hurt answer quality, not just waste latency/cost/tokens.
